title: Legal productivity: Speed gains exceed quality gains
desc: Shows assistance effects depend on task design and baseline performance, with users’ ability to identify benefit remaining contested.

kps.k: AI assistance often accelerates selected legal tasks more consistently than it improves substantive quality.
kps.d: The cluster primarily examines human performance with AI, rather than autonomous lawyer replacement. In Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, GPT-4 reduced completion time by 11.8–32.1% across four drafting tasks, but only contract drafting showed a statistically significant average quality gain at the 5% level. AI-Powered Lawyering found broader quality improvements with o1-preview and Vincent AI, alongside substantial time savings; neither tool significantly improved pooled accuracy. Its roughly 50–130% task-level productivity gains measure rubric scores relative to time used, not firm revenue or completed client matters. The translation experiment provides a nonlegal parallel: time fell 31.1%, while the quality increase remained statistically nonsignificant.

kps.k: Task design and the form of assistance matter more than a blanket distinction between easy and difficult work.
kps.d: AI Assistance in Legal Analysis found a 29-percentile-point multiple-choice gain but no average essay-grade improvement, with assisted answers sometimes missing hidden issues. Conversely, AI-Powered Lawyering located strong benefits in reasoning and advocacy but no overall benefit in template-based NDA drafting. The earlier GPT-4 drafting trial found its largest benefits in contract drafting, so these findings do not establish a general litigation-versus-transactional divide. Building a Better Lawyer further isolates interface design: highlighting made complaint review about 30% faster without measured quality loss; adding summaries reduced that advantage, and summaries alone did not accelerate work. Its authors recommend testing specific outputs rather than assuming that more assistance helps.

kps.k: AI can improve substantive synthesis and subsequent unaided reasoning, not merely polish prose.
kps.d: Artificial Intelligence and Human Legal Reasoning reports gains of 1.20 standard deviations in overall synthesis quality and 1.08 in substantive quality, alongside a 12.62% time reduction. Participants initially exposed to AI then performed 24.01% better on an application task completed without AI. The authors interpret the disappearance of the AI-exposure coefficient after controlling for synthesis performance as evidence that stronger foundational work supported later reasoning. This does not establish durable learning or independent skill development. Application productivity alone did not improve significantly, although the combined workflow produced better work in less time.

kps.k: Lower baseline performers often gain more, but neither universal equalization nor harm to experts follows.
kps.d: The GPT-4 drafting trial found larger quality gains for weaker participants on useful tasks, while speed savings remained broadly shared. Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier likewise reports performance gains of 43% for lower-ranked consultants and 17% for higher-ranked consultants on work inside AI's capability frontier; these ranks describe an already highly skilled sample. Some legal results suggest deterioration at the top: AI-assisted revision lowered scores for initially stronger memos, and the exam study reported declines among top students. However, the revision authors call their evidence limited, and the exam authors warn that mean reversion may largely explain the pattern. AI-Powered Lawyering's baseline-skill findings also coexist with little evidence of overall score-variance compression.

kps.k: The sources differ on whether users can accurately judge when AI helps.
kps.d: Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence found that participants' usefulness rankings matched measured task effects and inferred that firms could trust task-specific lawyer judgment rather than impose strict usage controls. Thinking Like a Lawyer, discussing the six-task reasoning/RAG experiment rather than an independent replication, emphasizes the opposite calibration problem: participants rated tools helpful even on the NDA task, which showed no measurable benefit. AI-Powered Lawyering also reports mismatches between perceived and measured tool advantages. The nonlegal Cognitive offloading study adds a distinct caution: participants underestimated assisted completion time by 57.8 seconds, and reported effort reductions on many more tasks than showed significant time savings. These findings distinguish satisfaction and reduced effort from demonstrated efficiency; they do not show that all perceived gains are illusory.

kps.k: Higher average quality can coexist with citation errors and missed legal issues.
kps.d: AI-Powered Lawyering records 18 citation-related incidents across 768 task submissions: three with Vincent AI, four without AI and eleven with o1-preview. Its category includes both fabricated sources and fundamentally misinterpreted real sources, so these counts are not pure model hallucination rates. The authors treat the small counts descriptively and regard any RAG reliability advantage as tentative. Artificial Intelligence and Human Legal Reasoning instead found few fabricated or misstated rules and no group difference in its setting. Together with the exam study's missed issues and rule variations, these results make checking authorities and legal substance a separate practical requirement from evaluating writing quality or speed.

kps.k: Implementation support may help translate tool access into useful practice, but reported gains are not measured service outcomes.
kps.d: Generative AI and Legal Aid reports that 90% of pilot participants perceived some productivity increase and 75% intended to continue using AI. Lawyers concentrated on applications they considered lower-risk, including summaries, preliminary research, accessible communication and first drafts. Concierge support correlated with better reported outcomes on most measures, though only three differences remained significant after adjustment for prior use. These findings support attention to access, training and workflow selection, but variable exposure and self-report limit conclusions about actual productivity. How the Billable Hour Can Survive Generative AI reuses this evidence rather than adding a replication, and notes that legal-aid lawyers typically do not bill hourly. Neither these reports nor the highlighting experiment demonstrates a reduction in unmet civil legal need or a firm-level billing outcome.

qs.q: Thus, even with the limitations discussed here, our findings suggest reason for optimism and rapid adoption of forms of AI assistance known to enhance efficiency and therefore likely to prove helpful in increasing access to legal work and to the justice system.

kps.k: The practical implication is targeted evaluation, not a universal productivity multiplier or an established replacement case.
kps.d: Randomized assignments, blind grading and robustness checks strengthen several studies, but student samples, simplified assignments, subjective rubrics and sometimes self-reported timing limit generalization to experienced practice. AI-Powered Lawyering additionally acknowledges fixed task order and unadjusted task-level multiple testing. Measures also differ: the consultant study times progress to a final question, not early completion of the whole assignment. Comparisons across model generations are not concurrent tests; AI-Powered Lawyering finds no systematic speed superiority over prior GPT-4 results. Predictions that sustained learning, specialized tools or combined reasoning and retrieval will produce larger gains remain forecasts. The evidence supports evaluating particular human–AI workflows for time, substantive quality and reliability before extrapolating to staffing, revenue or autonomous legal service delivery.

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources broadly accept the proposition that AI assistance accelerates selected legal tasks more consistently than it improves substantive quality. They materially develop it by identifying mechanisms and boundary conditions: outcomes vary by task, assistance format and baseline performance; speed or reduced effort must be distinguished from substantive quality; and higher average scores can coexist with missed issues or citation errors. Internal variation is material but does not amount to opposition. Some experiments find unusually large substantive gains in legal synthesis and downstream unaided reasoning, while others find no average essay improvement or no benefit on particular tasks. The sources also conflict on user calibration: one study found participants accurately ranked task usefulness, whereas later legal and nonlegal studies found substantial mismatches between perceived and measured benefits. These findings support targeted evaluation of particular human–AI workflows rather than a universal productivity multiplier or autonomous-replacement claim; because the corpus is curated, they should not be treated as representing all academic researchers.

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources accept the proposition’s core claim and materially develop it. Their common evidentiary pattern is that AI assistance produces clear gains in speed or task completion, whereas substantive-quality effects are smaller, less consistent, or dependent on the task. The legal drafting experiment reports significant time reductions across all four tasks but a significant average quality gain only for contract drafting; the nonlegal translation experiment similarly finds a 31.1% time reduction but no statistically significant quality increase. The sources extend this account by identifying mechanisms of variation: complaint highlighting accelerated review without measured quality loss, while summaries alone did not, showing that the form and amount of assistance matter; the consultant and legal-task studies also find larger performance gains among relatively lower-baseline participants. Material internal variation remains. The consultant experiment reports improvements in both completion and quality inside AI’s capability frontier and therefore does not independently establish that speed gains exceed quality gains. Its timing outcome measures progress to the final question rather than completion of the entire assignment. The legal drafting study also offers a relatively optimistic view of user calibration, because participants’ usefulness rankings matched measured task effects, while the broader cluster treats calibration as contested. Sample selection, simplified assignments, pooled models and task-specific measures further limit extrapolation to firm-wide productivity, autonomous legal work or universal performance gains.

qs.q: Discussion We find that the right kind of AI assistance can speed up the average rate of task completion on a realistic legal task while not affecting the means or distributions of measurements of the quality of legal work and process.
qs.a: Building a Better Lawyer: Experimental Evidence that AI Can Increase Legal Work Efficiency · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Rather we here experimentally demonstrate the importance of calibrating the amount and form of AI assistance provided during human-machine cooperation to complete a legal task.
qs.a: Building a Better Lawyer: Experimental Evidence that AI Can Increase Legal Work Efficiency · Academia · 2024

elens.an: The 2025 sources support the proposition that AI’s most consistent legal-productivity effect is faster completion of selected tasks, while substantive-quality effects depend on the task, tool and user. The legal-aid pilot reports perceived productivity gains concentrated in lower-risk uses and suggests that implementation support can help users overcome learning curves, but its outcomes are self-reported and do not establish measured service delivery, access-to-justice impact or autonomous lawyer replacement. The exam study supplies measured evidence of shorter completion times alongside no average essay-grade improvement, with benefits varying by question type and baseline performance and with qualitative weaknesses such as missed hidden issues. The billable-hour article adopts the same task-specific framing, but largely draws on existing studies rather than adding an independent replication. Material variation comes from the reasoning/RAG experiment, which found statistically significant quality gains on four of six tasks as well as speed gains; this strengthens rather than displaces the cluster’s account because another task showed no measurable benefit and the results remained tool- and task-dependent. That source also develops the cluster’s contested-calibration point: participants both perceived benefit where none was measured and underestimated benefits elsewhere. Taken together, this curated set supports targeted workflow evaluation and implementation assistance, not a universal productivity multiplier or a general replacement case.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that AI’s effects on legal productivity are task-specific and that speed gains are generally more consistent than substantive-quality gains, while materially extending it in two directions. First, the legal-task experiment attributes large quality-adjusted productivity increases chiefly to substantial time reductions combined with more modest average quality improvements; it also finds no significant pooled accuracy gain, no benefit on NDA drafting, persistent citation risks, and divergence between perceived and measured tool advantages. Second, the legal-synthesis experiment identifies an important exception: AI produced unusually large substantive-quality gains and better subsequent unaided reasoning, apparently by improving the foundational synthesis on which later work depended. That benefit did not generalize uniformly: application-task productivity was not significantly higher, and AI revision helped weaker memos while reducing scores for stronger ones. The nonlegal cognitive-offloading experiment further develops the cluster’s contested-calibration point by distinguishing lower perceived effort from actual speed: users substantially underestimated AI-assisted completion time, while significant acceleration appeared only on difficult tasks and a few individual tasks. Thus, this period’s evidence strengthens the case for evaluating particular human–AI workflows across time, substantive quality, reliability and user calibration rather than treating AI as a universal productivity multiplier. Internal variation concerns the balance of benefits—speed-dominant in the multi-task legal study, substantively quality-dominant in legal synthesis, and often effort-dominant rather than time-dominant in the nonlegal study—not rejection of the cluster’s principal proposition.
